Gogolin Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Gogolin, Poland

Not demolished. Jews began settling in Gogolin around 1845, belonging to the Opole kehilla due to their small numbers; population grew from 17 (1850) to 84 by 1880 before declining to 45 by 1921 and further as rising antisemitism drove most out in the early 1930s. This cemetery, established in 1857 on land donated by Meyer Fränkel, received its last burial (Moritz Hausdorf) on May 13, 1935. Ownership passed to the Jewish Association in Germany in 1939 and the Gestapo in 1943, though the site itself survived WWII undamaged; its funeral house was demolished in the early 1960s due to disrepair. A mass grave holds victims of forced-labor camps operating in Gogolin and Otmęt from 1940-1944, though it remains unmarked and its exact location unknown. The cemetery was originally separated from the adjoining Christian cemetery by a stone wall; both now appear as one combined site. About 20 sandstone matzevot and 50 tombstone bases survive, the oldest (1852) commemorating a deceased child, Emilia Stenger. The site entered Poland's Register of Monuments (no. 229/89) on December 4, 1989.
